sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** At-least-once delivery is the guarantee that each message will be delivered to the consumer one or more times — never silently lost — achieved by the consumer acknowledging (acking) the message only after successful processing, so that if the consumer crashes or the ack is lost, the broker redelivers the message until it receives a successful ack.

At-least-once delivery is the workhorse guarantee of message-queueing systems and the most common delivery semantic in production. The contract is simple: the broker will not remove a message from the queue until the consumer explicitly acknowledges successful processing; if the consumer crashes, the network drops the ack, or the processing times out, the broker redelivers the message to another consumer (or the same consumer after restart). This eliminates silent message loss — a critical property for any pipeline where losing a message means losing money, data, or user trust (payments, orders, audit logs, user actions). The cost is that the consumer may see the same message more than once: if the consumer processes the message successfully but the ack is lost in transit, the broker cannot distinguish "consumer crashed before processing" from "consumer processed but ack was lost" and must redeliver — the consumer will process the message again. This duplicate possibility is the fundamental trade-off of at-least-once: you get reliability (no losses) at the cost of duplicates, and the application must be designed to tolerate duplicates via idempotency. Kafka (default), AWS SQS, RabbitMQ, Google Pub/Sub, and most MQ systems default to at-least-once.

The mechanics of at-least-once center on the ack. When a consumer receives a message, it gets a "lease" or "visibility timeout" — a period (e.g., 30 seconds for SQS) during which the message is invisible to other consumers, giving the original consumer time to process. If the consumer finishes processing within the lease, it sends an ack (DeleteMessage in SQS, ack in RabbitMQ, commit offset in Kafka) and the broker removes the message permanently. If the consumer crashes or does not ack within the lease, the message becomes visible again and the broker redelivers it to another consumer. The lease is critical: too short (e.g., 1 second for a 10-second processing job) and the message is redelivered while the original consumer is still working, causing duplicate processing; too long (e.g., 1 hour) and a crashed consumer holds the message for an hour before redelivery, delaying recovery. The right lease is "expected processing time + safety margin" (e.g., 30s lease for a job that typically takes 5s but can occasionally take 20s). Kafka does not use a lease per se — it uses offset commits, where the consumer periodically commits its current offset and the broker retains all messages until they are old enough to be deleted by retention; redelivery happens if the consumer crashes before committing.

Real-world systems rely heavily on at-least-once. AWS SQS is the canonical at-least-once queue: messages are redelivered if not acked within the visibility timeout, with `ApproximateReceiveCount` exposed so consumers can detect duplicates. Kafka's default consumer is at-least-once: messages are redelivered if the consumer crashes before committing its offset (and the broker has not deleted the message due to retention). RabbitMQ acknowledgments (manual ack mode) give at-least-once: an unacked message is redelivered to another consumer on connection close. Google Pub/Sub offers at-least-once with a configurable ack deadline. All of these systems document the duplicate possibility explicitly — the AWS SQS documentation states "Amazon SQS provides at-least-once delivery, but occasionally a duplicate might be delivered." The architect's responsibility is to assume duplicates will happen and design consumers to be idempotent (covered in the exactly-once topic). Netflix's event pipeline, Uber's trip pipeline, and Amazon's order pipeline all run on at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers.

The key operational practice is **ack-after-processing, not ack-before-processing**. A common bug in at-least-once consumers is auto-acking on receive (or acking before processing completes): the broker removes the message, but if the consumer then crashes mid-processing, the message is lost — defeating the purpose of at-least-once. The correct pattern is manual ack: receive the message, process it fully (including all side effects like DB writes), then ack only after success. If processing fails (a transient error like a DB timeout), do not ack — let the broker redeliver. If processing fails permanently (a poison message that will never succeed), ack-and-route-to-DLQ to prevent infinite redelivery. The visibility timeout / lease must be longer than the worst-case processing time, or the broker will redeliver while the consumer is still working, causing concurrent duplicate processing. SQS extends this with `ChangeMessageVisibility` — a long-running consumer can extend the lease mid-processing if it knows it will take longer than the original timeout. Kafka consumers extend by simply not committing the offset until processing is done, with `max.poll.interval.ms` bounding the inactivity window.

The trade-off of at-least-once is between reliability, latency, and complexity. Compared to at-most-once (fire-and-forget, no ack), at-least-once adds one round-trip per message (the ack) and requires the broker to retain messages until acked, which adds storage and bookkeeping. Compared to exactly-once, at-least-once is simpler — no idempotency keys, no dedup tables, no transactional boundaries — but pushes the duplicate-handling burden to the consumer, which must be idempotent. For most pipelines, at-least-once + idempotent consumer is the right choice: the broker handles the reliability (no losses), and the consumer handles the duplicates (no double-charges). The architect's rule: default to at-least-once for any pipeline where losing a message is unacceptable, ensure the consumer is idempotent (or accept duplicates), set the visibility timeout to cover worst-case processing, and use a DLQ for poison messages. Reserve at-most-once for low-value telemetry (metrics, logs) where duplicates would be noise and losses are tolerable; reserve exactly-once for high-stakes financial transactions where duplicates are unacceptable even with idempotency.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant B as Broker
    participant C1 as Consumer A
    participant C2 as Consumer B
    P->>B: send msg
    B->>C1: deliver msg (lease=30s, invisible to others)
    Note over C1: processing... (crash before ack)
    Note over B: lease expires, msg visible again
    B->>C2: redeliver msg (to another consumer)
    C2->>C2: process successfully
    C2->>B: ack
    Note over B: remove msg permanently
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +-------+      send msg        +---------+
   | Prod  |--------------------->|         |
   +-------+                      | Broker  |
                                  | (queue) |
                                  +----+----+
                                       |
        deliver (lease=30s, invisible to others)
                                       |
                                       v
                                  +---------+
                                  |Consumer |  process... (crash!)
                                  |   A     |  (no ack sent)
                                  +---------+
                                       X (crashed)
                                       |
        lease expires -> msg visible again
                                       |
                                       v
                                  +---------+
                                  |Consumer |  process successfully
                                  |   B     |  ack -----------------> Broker
                                  +---------+                       (remove msg)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The producer sends a message to the broker, which delivers it to Consumer A with a 30-second lease — during the lease, no other consumer can see the message, giving A exclusive access.
2. Consumer A processes the message but crashes before sending the ack. The broker does not receive the ack, and when the lease expires, the message becomes visible again to other consumers.
3. The broker redelivers the message to Consumer B, which processes it successfully and sends an ack. The broker removes the message permanently. End result: the message was delivered twice (to A and B), but processed once successfully.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import time
import threading
from collections import deque

class AtLeastOnceQueue:
    """Queue with visibility-timeout-based redelivery for at-least-once."""
    def __init__(self, visibility_timeout=2.0):
        self.visibility_timeout = visibility_timeout
        self.messages = deque()       # (msg_id, payload, visible_at, acked)
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def send(self, msg_id, payload):
        with self.lock:
            self.messages.append([msg_id, payload, time.time(), False])

    def receive(self):
        """Receive a visible message; mark it invisible for visibility_timeout."""
        with self.lock:
            now = time.time()
            for m in self.messages:
                if not m[3] and m[2] <= now:
                    m[2] = now + self.visibility_timeout  # hide until timeout
                    return (m[0], m[1])
            return None

    def ack(self, msg_id):
        with self.lock:
            for m in self.messages:
                if m[0] == msg_id:
                    m[3] = True
                    return True
            return False

    def cleanup(self):
        with self.lock:
            self.messages = deque(m for m in self.messages if not m[3])

class Consumer:
    def __init__(self, name, queue, fail_first_n=0):
        self.name = name
        self.queue = queue
        self.fail_first_n = fail_first_n
        self.processed = []

    def process_once(self):
        msg = self.queue.receive()
        if not msg:
            return False
        msg_id, payload = msg
        # Simulate processing (or crash before ack)
        if len(self.processed) < self.fail_first_n:
            print(f"  [{self.name}] crash on {msg_id} (no ack)")
            return True  # crashed, did not ack -> will be redelivered
        self.processed.append(msg_id)
        print(f"  [{self.name}] processed {msg_id}: {payload}, ack")
        self.queue.ack(msg_id)
        return True

# Demo: Consumer A crashes on first attempt, Consumer B succeeds on redelivery
q = AtLeastOnceQueue(visibility_timeout=0.5)
q.send("m1", "order-99")

a = Consumer("A", q, fail_first_n=1)   # A crashes on first attempt
b = Consumer("B", q, fail_first_n=0)   # B always succeeds

print("Attempt 1 (Consumer A crashes):")
a.process_once()

print("\nWaiting for lease to expire...")
time.sleep(0.6)

print("\nAttempt 2 (Consumer B succeeds on redelivery):")
b.process_once()

print("\nFinal queue state (should be empty - msg acked):")
q.cleanup()
print(f"  remaining: {len(q.messages)} msgs")
print(f"  A processed: {a.processed}, B processed: {b.processed}")
```

quiz.question: What does "at-least-once delivery" guarantee, and what does it not guarantee?
options: Choose at-least-once when losing a message is unacceptable: payments, orders, audit logs, user actions, anything where loss means lost revenue or broken invariants.
The consumer processed 300 messages but did not commit the offset, so on restart it resumes from the last committed offset — re-reading and re-processing all 500…
Idempotency means processing the same message multiple times has the same effect as processing it once.
(3) Bounded delivery time — if the consumer is slow or down, delivery is delayed indefinitely (until retention expires).
quiz.explanation: At-least-once delivery guarantees that each message will be delivered to the consumer one or more times — never zero times (no silent loss). It does not guarantee exactly-once: the consumer may see the same message multiple times if the broker redelivers due to a lost ack, a consumer crash, or a visibility-timeout expiry during processing.

quiz.question: Why is "ack after processing" critical in at-least-once consumers?
options: Idempotency means processing the same message multiple times has the same effect as processing it once.
The visibility timeout is the period during which a delivered message is invisible to other consumers, giving the original consumer exclusive time to process.
Choose at-least-once when losing a message is unacceptable: payments, orders, audit logs, user actions, anything where loss means lost revenue or broken invariants.
The ack is the consumer's signal to the broker that the message has been processed successfully and can be removed.
quiz.explanation: The ack is the consumer's signal to the broker that the message has been processed successfully and can be removed. If the consumer acks before processing completes (e.g., on receive, or mid-processing), and then crashes before finishing, the broker has already removed the message — it is lost, defeating the entire purpose of at-least-once.

The visibility timeout is the period during which a delivered message is invisible to other consumers, giving the original consumer exclusive time to process.
quiz.explanation: The visibility timeout is the period during which a delivered message is invisible to other consumers, giving the original consumer exclusive time to process. SQS calls it "visibility timeout" (default 30s, max 12h); RabbitMQ uses "consumer prefetch" with ack timeouts; Kafka uses max.poll.interval.ms. When a consumer receives a message, the broker hides it from other consumers for the timeout duration.

quiz.question: How does Kafka's at-least-once consumer work?
options: The visibility timeout (3s) is shorter than the processing time (5s), so the broker will redeliver the message after 3 seconds — while the original consumer is still…
The migration involves several changes: (1) Producer: switch from UDP send-to-broker to Kafka producer with acks=all (wait for all in-sync replicas) and retries enabled…
The vast majority of production message-queueing systems default to at-least-once.
Kafka's consumer is at-least-once by default.
quiz.explanation: Kafka's consumer is at-least-once by default. The consumer reads messages from a partition in order, processes them, and periodically commits its current offset (the position in the partition it has processed up to). The broker retains all messages for the retention period (default 7 days), so even committed messages can be re-read by seeking backward.

quiz.question: How do you make an at-least-once consumer idempotent?
options: Kafka's consumer is at-least-once by default.
Use Kafka with the user ID as the partition key — all messages for a given user go to the same partition, and Kafka delivers them in order within the partition.
The migration involves several changes: (1) Producer: switch from UDP send-to-broker to Kafka producer with acks=all (wait for all in-sync replicas) and retries enabled…
Idempotency means processing the same message multiple times has the same effect as processing it once.
quiz.explanation: Idempotency means processing the same message multiple times has the same effect as processing it once. There are several patterns: (1) Natural idempotency: the side effect is inherently idempotent — e.g., UPDATE users SET status='active' WHERE id=42 produces the same result whether run once or twice. No dedup needed.
